title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement:
You are given the root of a binary tree and you stand on its right side, looking at it. At each depth you can see only the node that is furthest to the right on that level; nodes on that level further left are hidden behind it. A node in a left subtree is visible when the right side of that level has no node, which happens when the right subtree is shorter than the left one.

Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from the top level (the root) to the bottom level. The tree has at least one node.

**Follow-up:** interviewers asked for both BFS and DFS solutions. Meta also asked a variation that returns the left view as well as the right view, with a different ordering for each side (for example the left view top to bottom and the right view bottom to top). Only the plain right-side view is tested here.
input_format: A single line with the tree in level order: the root first, then for each node in that order its left child and its right child, using `null` for a missing child. Children of `null` entries are not listed, and trailing `null` values may be omitted. Tokens are separated by spaces.
output_format: Print the visible values from top to bottom, separated by spaces, on one line.

examples.explanation: Level 0 shows 7. On level 1 the right-most node is 9. Level 2 contains 1 (under 3) and 6 (under 9); 6 is further right. Level 3 contains only 2, the left child of 6.
Level 1 shows 6. Node 6 has no children, so on level 2 only the children of 2 exist (1 and 4), and 4 is the right-most of them, even though it is in the left subtree.

complexity.space: O(w) where w is the maximum width of the tree (O(h) for a DFS)

hints: Think level by level. Which node on each level is the one you can see?
A BFS that processes one level at a time gives you the last node of each level directly.
A DFS also works: visit the right child before the left child, and record a node's value the first time you reach a new depth.
